{{Short description|Statistical model}}
The '''ACE model''' is a [[statistical model]] commonly used to analyze the results of [[twin studies|twin]] and [[adoption studies]]. This classic [[Behavioural genetics|behaviour genetic]] model aims to partition the [[phenotypic]] [[variance]] into three categories: [[additive genetic effects|additive genetic variance]] (A), common (or shared) environmental factors (C), and specific (or nonshared) environmental factors plus [[measurement error]] (E).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Germine |first1=Laura |last2=Russell |first2=Richard |last3=Bronstad |first3=P. Matthew |last4=Blokland |first4=Gabriëlla A.M. |last5=Smoller |first5=Jordan W. |last6=Kwok |first6=Holum |last7=Anthony |first7=Samuel E. |last8=Nakayama |first8=Ken |last9=Rhodes |first9=Gillian |date=October 2015 |title=Individual Aesthetic Preferences for Faces Are Shaped Mostly by Environments, Not Genes |journal=Current Biology |volume=25 |issue=20 |pages=2684–2689 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2015.08.048 |issn=0960-9822 |pmc=4629915 |pmid=26441352|bibcode=2015CBio...25.2684G }}</ref> It is widely used in [[genetic epidemiology]] and [[behavioural genetics]].<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia  |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd |location=Chichester, UK |last=Maes |first=Hermine H. |title=Encyclopedia of Statistics in Behavioral Science |chapter=ACE Model |date=2005-10-15 |language=en |doi=10.1002/0470013192.bsa002 |isbn=978-0470860809  }}</ref><ref name=bsb>{{Cite journal |last1=Kohler |first1=Hans-Peter |last2=Behrman |first2=Jere R. |last3=Schnittker |first3=Jason |date=2011 |title=Social science methods for twins data: integrating causality, endowments, and heritability |journal=Biodemography and Social Biology |volume=57 |issue=1 |pages=88–141 |doi=10.1080/19485565.2011.580619 |issn=1948-5565 |pmc=3158495 |pmid=21845929}}</ref> The basic ACE model relies on several assumptions, including the absence of [[assortative mating]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beauchamp |first1=Jonathan P. |last2=Cesarini |first2=David |last3=Johannesson |first3=Magnus |last4=Lindqvist |first4=Erik |last5=Apicella |first5=Coren |date=2010-07-06 |title=On the sources of the height–intelligence correlation: New insights from a bivariate ACE model with assortative mating |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=242–252 |doi=10.1007/s10519-010-9376-7 |issn=0001-8244 |pmc=3044837 |pmid=20603722}}</ref> that there is no [[genetic dominance]] or [[epistasis]],<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FShOTUIfxwwC |title=Family Matters: Designing, Analysing and Understanding Family Based Studies in Life Course Epidemiology |last1=Lawlor |first1=Debbie A. |last2=Lawlor |first2=Deborah A. |last3=Mishra |first3=Gita D. |date=2009-04-02 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=9780199231034 |pages=252–3 |language=en}}</ref> that all genetic effects are additive, and the absence of [[gene-environment interaction]]s.<ref name=bsb/> In order to address these limitations, several variants of the ACE model have been developed, including an ACE-β model, which emphasizes the identification of causal effects,<ref name=bsb/> and the ACDE model, which accounts for the effects of [[dominance (genetics)|genetic dominance]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Xueqin |last2=Guo |first2=Xiaobo |last3=He |first3=Mingguang |last4=Zhang |first4=Heping |date=2011-02-09 |title=Statistical Inference in Mixed Models and Analysis of Twin and Family Data
